item.title: “I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam”
item.description:
“I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam”

July 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Originally from the Philippines, Deepa Paul moved to Amsterdam nearly 15 years ago after her husband took a job in the capital. Her book about opening up her marriage, Ask Me How It Works, was longlisted for the Women’s Prize for Non-Fiction. She loves how the Dutch do kids birthday parties, strongly advises tourists not to cycle and wishes she could have met Mata Hari.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?
I was born in the Philippines to a Bengali father and Filipina mother. I met my husband at university in Manila. I was studying communication but also had a crazy pipe dream of going to Europe to train as a classical singer. His first job ended up being in Singapore, so we had a long-distance relationship for four years while I lived in Manila. After we were married, I moved to Singapore to be with him and found work as a writer and producer in TV. But Singapore wasn’t really my bag.

I pitched my husband the idea of one last adventure before having a baby: a round-the-world trip, him on unpaid sabbatical, me writing freelance. He thought I was crazy and suggested finding a job abroad instead.

A friend working at a Dutch multinational offered to put him in touch with a VP at their Amsterdam HQ. I remember thinking that the cold email my husband wrote sounded way too direct and maybe a bit too much. Turns out the Dutch are a direct culture: it worked! One job offer and six months later, we were on a one-way flight to Amsterdam.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?
I am an immigrant.

How long do you plan to stay?
I don’t see an end date. I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam, although I often fantasise about living a parallel existence somewhere warm in the winter.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?
There’s nothing glamorous about how I accumulated the Dutch I speak now, which I’d describe as pretty passable for daily social life. It was one awkward conversation with one school parent at a time, lots of listening to how people actually talk, and relying on context clues to fill in the 20-30% I might not be grasping accurately when people talk fast.

My husband had negotiated 30 hours of Dutch lessons for both of us, through his employer, when he started his job. I paused for a year or two after I gave birth to my daughter, then went back and took classes at the Volksuniversiteit.

I find that when Dutch people switch to English with me, I can push back. My go-to phrase is ‘ik ben grappiger in het Engels’ [I’m funnier in English]. Humour is disarming, it smooths over the switch in social situations..

My greatest achievement was being interviewed live on NPO Radio 1 about my book in Dutch. The segment was only supposed to last 8 minutes, but it was the longest 11 minutes of my life! Turns out talking about love, commitment, sex and open marriage is far more complicated than chatting about the weather.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?
You’re asking a polyamorist to choose just one?! I love the mobility and freedom of cycling. Gezelligheid. The simplicity of young children’s birthday parties. The straightforward ease of voting — if you don’t come from a culture of systemically corrupt and murderous elections, as I do, you might not appreciate what a privilege and relief that is. The progression of flowers in the spring, from tulips to hyacinths to cherry blossoms to peonies to roses to dahlias: what a gift it is to have a reliable abundance of beauty.

How Dutch have you become?
Not much — I’m still too short (1.56m). I would argue that living in the Netherlands has given me the space and independence to become more myself, rather than more Dutch.

Having said that, I am a lot more direct now, and I not only can handle direct communication, I prefer it. It’s quite a relief actually, coming from a conflict-avoidant, high-context culture. I’ve been nearly cured of my lifelong affliction of Filipino time, which means I’m only mildly late most of the time, and actually punctual the rest of the time.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?
Anne Frank, who inspired me to start keeping a journal at the age of nine. She was the first person to show me that writing about my inner world and observing my own life, no matter how small and ordinary, is a worthy endeavour.

Rachel Ruysch, the most prolific and commercially successful female artist of the Dutch Golden Age, whose floral still life paintings sold for more than Rembrandt’s paintings in that time.

Mata Hari, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in Friesland, a bold free spirit who harnessed her eroticism, feminine power and artistic expression to live a courageous life and extraordinary life for a woman of her time. Later biographies exonerated her of espionage in World War I, but her image as a powerful and mysterious femme fatale endures to this day.

What’s your top tourist tip?
Please don’t cycle in Amsterdam, especially not with your selfie stick out. It’s not Disneyland with tulips and windmills along every cycle path. Some of us have things to do and places to get to.

On a less grumpy note, try to book a visit to the Six Collection in advance. It’s a private art collection that spans over three centuries and 10 generations of the wealthy and influential Six family, who have one of the most celebrated Rembrandt paintings you’ve never seen hanging right in their living room.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.
When I gave birth in 2013, I was taken aback that official paternity leave was two days — one day for the actual birth and a second day for the father to register it. It ran completely counter to the image of the Netherlands in my mind as egalitarian, progressive and liberal. It turns out that it’s still deeply patriarchal in small, hidden and entrenched ways.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?
If I’m not panicking about making sure everything is packed and ready to go, cycle around my neighbourhood and have a coffee at my favourite spots. If the weather allows, go for a walk and read in the sunshine at Westerpark, then go for a dip in the IJ.

Throw a big party at home for all the friends I’ve made over the last 15 years, all the people who have become part of my story (except those I’ve revoked access to). My husband will cook enough Filipino food to feed everyone one last time. Eat, drink, laugh, cry, hug and dance, maybe stay up talking until the sun comes up.

If we make it out early enough, go dancing until my legs give out or the club kicks us out. Cycle home as the sun rises and enjoy one last sleep in my own bed—or not.

Deepa was speaking to Molly Quell.

Ask Me How It Works is available for sale at the American Book Center. You can follow Deepa on Substack and Instagram.

item.title: Drugs baron Bolle Jos convicted in absentia in Belgium
item.description:
Drugs baron Bolle Jos convicted in absentia in Belgium

July 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch drug criminal Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, has been convicted by a Belgian judge and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

The 35-year old was not present at the court in Antwerp when the verdict was announced on Thursday, having been on the run since 2024.

Leijdekkers was sentenced for his part in the Costa drugs case, in which a total of 56 people were accused of smuggling 25 tonnes of cocaine through Antwerp and money laundering. The drugs had a street value of €3.5 billion.

An investigation by Follow The Money revealed that the Brabant drugs baron has been living in Sierre Leone and is in a relationship with the president’s daughter.

Two years ago, a Dutch judge sentenced him to 24 years in 2024 for cocaine trafficking through the ports of Antwerp and Rotterdam.

In total, he has been sentenced to 103 years in prison across 10 trials.

The Dutch have requested his extradition from Sierre Leone, but the government denies any knowledge of his presence in the country.

According to drugs experts, the West African country has become a major logistical hub for the smuggling of drugs from South America to Europe.

Earlier this year, Spanish authorities intercepted a ship that had departed from the country and discovered 30,215 kilograms of cocaine, the largest intercepted cocaine shipment ever.

item.title: More sluice gates close but no national drought measures yet
item.description:
More sluice gates close but no national drought measures yet

July 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

No national drought restrictions will be imposed immediately despite coastal water boards taking steps to keep sea water out of river mouths and the Rhine dropping to its lowest ever level.

At a weekly meeting to discuss the ongoing water shortage, regional authorities agreed to work together to ensure the “most efficient distribution possible” of water and announced local measures to protect drinking water.

The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, the point where the river crosses the Dutch border, has dropped to less than 700 m3 per second, one-third of its normal level for July and an unprecedentedly low rate.

River cruise operators have had to cancel or shorten their excursions on the Rhine, while water authorities are considering introducing restrictions such as one-way traffic to prevent ships becoming stuck in the shallow water. Such measures would extend delivery times or force freight companies to transport cargo by road.

The Netherlands is currently at level two on a three-stage scale of water shortages, which authorises officials in the ministry to hold crisis talks. An actual crisis is level three.

The canal locks at Eefde, which gives access to the Twentekanaal, closed for the first time because of drought on Friday. Local businesses say the closure of the sluice gates, which carry 15,000 to 20,000 ships a year, will have an impact on the economy around Almelo, Enschede and Hengelo.

Harsh measures

“We understand this is necessary for security, but it’s a harsh measure,” said Frank van Zomeren. manager of the Port of Twente Bornebroek.

Deventer is closing its harbour to shipping this weekend for the first time in eight years because the IJssel has dropped below safe levels.

In the west, Delfland water authority has restricted the opening of the Parksluizen gates between the Nieuw Maas and the Schie to prevent sea water encroaching on the river mouth.

Sluice gates at Maassluis, Schiedam and Vlaardingen were closed last week. Other authorities are also imposing restrictions to prevent drinking water becoming contaminated.

Recreational swimmers have been warned to look out for blue-green algae, technically known as cyanobacteria, which grows faster in warm water and can cause skin irritation or sicknesses such as diarrhoea if swallowed.

item.title: Germany seeks extradition of Dutch man accused of hotel murder
item.description:
Germany seeks extradition of Dutch man accused of hotel murder

July 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

German authorities will ask the Netherlands to extradite a 42-year-old man from Almelo who is suspected of killing a disabled man in a hotel near the border.

The body of the 35-year-old victim was found by staff at Hotel Rheinpark in Rees, a town beside the Rhine 30km south of Doetinchem, on Sunday morning after the pair failed to check out.

A postmortem examination confirmed that the victim, who had a physical disability and used a wheelchair, had been strangled.

The two men had checked in the night before after going to see a fireworks show in the area, German media reported.

Only the victim’s details were registered at check-in, leading police to launch an appeal for the suspect, who had fled back across the border in the victim’s car, according to local media. He was arrested later on Tuesday in Almelo.

German police have confirmed they will be seeking the extradition of the 42-year-old man to face trial for murder after issuing a European arrest warrant.

RTV Oost reported that the suspect, identified as L., was known as a hardcore supporter of Almelo football club Heracles. He was known by the nickname Visbom after he allegedly once threw an object at a goalkeeper.

item.title: One person dies, six injured in crash between lorry and minibus
item.description:
One person dies, six injured in crash between lorry and minibus

July 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

One person has died and six others have been seriously injured in a head-on collision between a minibus and a lorry in Overijssel.

The crash happened on the N48 near Balkbrug, around 20km east of Zwolle, at around 11.30am on Thursday. All the victims were sitting in the minibus, which had Belgian numberplates.

Fire appliances, ambulances and an air ambulance were called to the crash site. Six passengers were taken to different hospitals in the area, while the seventh was pronounced dead at the scene. The lorry driver was unharmed.

The road is likely to be closed for several hours while police carry out investigations and the road is cleared of debris.

item.title: University launches ethics probe into Red Bull professor’s work
item.description:
University launches ethics probe into Red Bull professor’s work

July 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Utrecht University has begun an investigation into its pharmacology department after a professor was accused of not declaring payments for research from companies, including energy drinks manufacturer Red Bull.

Joris Verster published several papers on energy drinks and alcohol in his capacity as associate professor, without disclosing that he was also paid as a consultant for Red Bull and US-based Sen-Jam Pharmaceuticals.

The university does not prohibit consultancy work, but academics are required to disclose any relevant secondary activities when they publish papers under conflict of interest rules.

The investigation follows reports in several Dutch and international media outlets, including Trouw, De Groene Amsterdammer and Investico, that Verster’s research was published without any reference to his paid work for Red Bull and Sen-Jam.

Verster set up a private company, NeuroClinics, for his consultancy work, which frequently overlapped with his academic research.

Hangover pill

He carried out a study into a hangover pill produced by Sen-Jam which concluded, based on a questionnaire circulated around his students, that the medicine did not encourage people to consume more alcohol.

Mariëtte van den Hoven, professor of medical ethics at Amsterdam’s UMC medical centre, said Verster’s methods amounted to a conflict of interest “by using the university to promote your personal goals.”

Another study, published in 2010, concluded that drinking a can of Red Bull improved driving performance, based on observing drivers for four hours in a simulator. It was publicised under the heading “Can Red Bull fuel better driving?”

Verster also published research that disputed claims that mixing energy drinks with alcohol were damaging to people’s health and could lead to aggressive behaviour or unsafe sexual practices.

His conclusion was that combining the drinks meant users consumed less alcohol and were less prone to reckless behaviour.

Sick leave

Verster himself, who has been on sick leave since the start of May, told Trouw he had always been transparent about his private work.

“I have been a consultant for many companies and stated it in all my papers, even when it concerned a minor role,” he said. “I informed Utrecht University about my work as a consultant and the university approved it.”

item.title: Eighth species of American crayfish found in Dutch rivers
item.description:
Eighth species of American crayfish found in Dutch rivers

July 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A new species of crayfish has been found in Dutch rivers, the eighth type to establish itself in the Netherlands after being introduced in the upper Rhine.

The calico crayfish (Faxonius immunis), originally from North America, was spotted in Gelderland by ecologist Pim Lemmers, who first encountered the creatures in a nature reserve near Karlsruhe decades ago.

“I’d been expecting them and looking out for them for a while,” he told NOS. “Last year I found a crayfish pincer and I knew straight away that it might be a significant one.“

The discovery of the pincer, together with the results of DNA samples, are enough to confirm that the crayfish have made it to the Dutch river system.

The water authority in Rivierland has reported the presence of the crayfish to the food standards regulator NVWA, which will in turn notify the European Union, and triggered the protocol for dealing with invasive exotic species.

The Dutch agriculture ministry has set up a working group to investigate how the crayfish can be prevented from spreading. Crayfish damage the local environment by eating indigenous plants and animals and digging in river banks.

“We’re at a very uncertain stage, because are they just in the Klompenwaard area of the Rhine or are they already in our regional waters? Can we keep them out of the waters?” said José Vos, senior policy adviser for the water board.

item.title: Post-Covid fatigue not just caused by inactivity, study finds
item.description:
Post-Covid fatigue not just caused by inactivity, study finds

July 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Patients with post-Covid syndrome suffer muscle damage that cannot be fully be explained by inactivity, research led by scientists at Amsterdam’s Vrije Universiteit (VU) has found.

The team compared the blood and muscle tissue of patients with long Covid and chronic fatigue (ME) with a group of healthy people who spent 60 days in bed as part of a study simulating the effects of space travel.

The post-Covid and ME patients had suffered from energy dips that caused them to avoid exercising or spend long periods in bed, which has a degrading impact on the skeletal muscles.

But the researchers, led by Rob Wüst, a movement scientist at the VU, found differences in the colour of the muscle fibres between the two groups, indicating that the post-Covid patients had a much lower oxygen capacity.

“As skeletal muscle characteristics differ between patients and healthy individuals after bed rest, physical inactivity cannot solely explain the lower exercise capacity and skeletal muscle adaptations in long Covid and ME/CFS patients,” they wrote in a paper published in Nature Communications.

The healthy individuals from the space programme still had bright red fibres, which are still oxygen-rich, while the patients had white fibres, which become exhausted much faster.

Rapid tiredness

The researchers said the difference could explain why post-Covid and ME sufferers become tired so quickly even after modest levels of exercise or exertion. “The redder the fibres, the more stamina a person has,” Wüst explained.

Lung specialist Merel Hellemons, of the Erasmus MC teaching hospital in Rotterdam, told the Volkskrant that the findings were a crucial development in understanding how to treat patients with conditions such as post-Covid syndrome.

“Many patients hear that they need to move more or that being less active is bad for them,” she said.

Wüst said patients should still be encouraged to be more mobile to avoid damage to their muscles, skeletons and cardiovascular system caused by inactivity. “The question is: what is possible? We need more tailored solutions,” he said.

item.title: Profits at KLM up in 2026 despite fuel cost increases
item.description:
Profits at KLM up in 2026 despite fuel cost increases

July 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch airline KLM booked a higher-than-expected profit in the first half of the year, despite the rise in fuel prices caused by ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

The company reported revenue of €6.9 bn in the six months to June, an 8% increase compared to the same period last year.

The airline benefited from a decrease in flights from competitors like Qatar Airways and Emirates because of the unrest in the region.

“The measures we are implementing are having a positive impact on our results,” CEO Marjan Rintel said in a statement.

Those measures included passing on higher fuel prices to customers, particularly on long-haul flights.

Yesterday, the Air France-KLM airline group announced they had put in an offer for a stake in Portugal’s TAP airline. Lisbon said last year that it was seeking a major international airline to buy most of the 49.9 percent stake that it planned to sell.

German airline Lufthansa also submitted a bid.

item.title: Man who strangled partner jailed after new forensic method used
item.description:
Man who strangled partner jailed after new forensic method used

July 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A man has been convicted of attempting to kill his partner in the first case to use new techniques to detect signs of strangulation in domestic violence.

The 33-year-old man from Rozenburg grabbed the woman by the neck as an argument turned violent last November. Police were alerted by neighbours and pulled the man away from his victim, who later said she was “turning blue”.

She was examined by a medical specialist using a new procedure developed in Rotterdam to gather forensic evidence faster in suspected cases of strangulation.

The doctor said the attack could have been fatal if it was prolonged, a detail that allowed prosecutors to argue that the attack should be classed as attempted manslaughter.

The procedure was introduced last December to try to detect strangulation, which is seen as an early warning sign of femicide, in domestic abuse investigations before the victim’s injuries heal and the evidence disappears.

200 referrals

The medical agency FARR, based in Rotterdam, anticipated receiving 200 inquiries a year, but was called on 150 times in the first three months. In 92% of cases doctors concluded the injuries could have been caused by strangulation. Nine in 10 victims were female and 78% of inquiries were related to domestic violence.

“It’s a huge number,” the agency’s managing director Geranda Zeelenberg told NOS. “Previously we hardly ever saw these people. They were probably always there, but the research we’ve begun has increased awareness of these cases.”

The man from Rozenburg was sentenced to 360 days in prison for attempted manslaughter, including 169 days suspended, and a community service order of 150 hours, in line with the prosecution’s demands.

His lawyer told the court he had no recollection of the events on the night of the attack because he had been taking alcohol and amphetamines, but argued that he had attacked her to try to force her to have sex rather than attempting to kill her.
